content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a method for open-world instance recognition tasks. The proposed model was built upon the Deformable-DETR with several proposed changes by the authors. The main proposed components and contributions are highlighted in Table 6 (ablation study). While some of the proposed components are from existing work (not within the context of open-world instance segmentation or object detection), they do show some novelty in the proposed components. The resultant model demonstrated comparable or state-of-the-art performance when compared to existing approaches across 4 various settings.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## Pros
- The presentation flow of the paper is very good, and it's easy to follow.
- The simple ablation study in Table 1 clearly demonstrates the benefit of the proposed stop-grad method
- Ablation study in Table 6 showed the effectiveness of each proposed component and provide insights into future works
- The figure illustration and captions are informative. 
- The proposed method consists of several components added on top of the Deformable-DETR is considered to be somewhat novel in my opinion. It opens another door for future work.

## Cons
- The performance of the proposed model seems to be less satisfied in Tables 2 and 3 without teacher-student pseudo-labeling. However, when adding pseudo-labeling, it is also not effective in Tables 4 and 5. This hinders the overall effectiveness of the proposed method as a whole.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- It's not clear to me how k1 and k2 are selected in Eq. (3). Are they decided through a certain rule? I was not able to find the details describing it in the main paper or in the Appendix, but I think this is an extremely important part of the proposed method.
- I am a bit confused after reading Sec. 3.4, where the authors proposed to use their proposed SWORD model as a teacher to train the close-world model by generating pseudo-labels. I believe the main benefit of doing this is that jointly training the pseudo-labels generated by the teacher SWORD model and ground-truth annotation will significantly boost the performance of the model. If so, I think the authors should first make it clear that this is developed because of boosting performance and it was following existing practice, e.g., from GGN. However, on the other hand, I also saw that adding pseudo-labels does not universally generalize to other experimental settings, e.g., Tables 4 and 5.
- Choosing how we generate pseudo-labels has been a critical part of any projects that use pseudo-labeling techniques, especially the ones that use hard pseudo-labels. In Fig. 4, the authors experimented with a top-k selection of pseudo-labels. Historically, top-k selection for pseudo-labels does not generalize and is very use-case dependent. After reading Appendix C, I am still wondering if the authors have tried other pseudo-label generation methods, like thresholding or even soft pseudo-labels (this might be hard to add pseudo-labels with ground-truth annotations). For example, how about we use the box IoU score to select pseudo-labels, instead of discarding them with 0.5 thresholding and then selecting top-k?

- The authors cited Mask2Former paper in Sec. 3.2 when discussing adding a mask head to the Deformable-DETR. Will the proposed method apply to Mask2Former? What are the challenges if we do so?
- How does this work relate to Detic (Detecting Twenty-thousand Classes using Image-level Supervision)? While they are not directly comparable, I think it might be worth discussing the differences and shared merits between the two works/directions.

- It would be great if the authors provide a little bit more explanation of stop-grad in the intro section. Currently, it's hard to grasp what it is without reading the method section (especially before reading FIg. 2 b).
- I would encourage the authors to put in accuracy gain the experimental result tables so that the readers understand what the authors are referring to when specific improvement numbers in the text (e.g., in Sec. 4.2.)
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, I think this is a nicely written paper with some findings that are worth to be shared with the research community. While the proposed method is not strictly technical novel, there are empirical novelty aspects of the paper that I enjoyed reading. At this point, I am rating this paper marginally above the acceptance threshold and have raised a couple of questions that I still think it's important to discuss during the rebuttal stage. I will review the replies from the authors and adjust my rating accordingly.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper works on the problem of open-world instance segmentation, i.e., segmenting un-annotated objects outside of the training classes. The authors identified two key issues and addressed them: 1. novel objects are sometimes trained as background, and the authors propose to stop gradient from the classifier to the backbone; 2. how to distinguish un-annotated objects from background, the authors proposed a contrastive-learning-based loss that automatically split a set of proposals into clustered foreground and scattered background. Experiments on several customized show the proposed framework outperforms a close-world baseline.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength

+ The paper works on an important and challenging problem: open-world instance segmentation. The overall ideas of stop-classification-gradient and contrastive learning are reasonable and make sense to me.

+ The paper provides good baselines for the new UVO dataset.

+ The title is cool.


Weaknesses:

- My first complaint is the benchmark selection. Most experiments use COCO (80 classes) as the base classes. Conceptually, I feel it hard to learn a general enough object concept on 80 classes, especially when evaluating on LVIS which has >1000 classes. As a results, all the numbers in this paper are low (compared to the fully supervised model). This makes me feel we are making tiny progresses on a weak baseline and it is still far from solving the problem. Personally I like the benchmark used in ViLD (Gu et al. ICLR 2022), which uses ~800 classes from LVIS as base classes and ~400 classes as novel classes.

- The paper contains a mixture of technical components, including stop-gradient, one-to-many assignment, adding class scores, contrastive learning (Table. 6), and teacher-student learning (Sec. 3.4). However the introduction only highlights two: stop-gradient and contrastive learning. From Table 6 it looks like one-to-any assignment matters much more than stop-gradient, which makes the takeaway unclear. I suggest the authors to clearly separate existing techniques (e.g., IoU score, self-training etc.) and novel technics, put all existing techniques into the baseline, and only ablate the new components.

- It's still unclear to me why stop-gradient on classification head help open-world generalization. Is it simply because multi-task learning of proposal and classification hurts proposal? If this is the case, should using different networks for proposal and classification be more helpful? Note this is NOT a required experiments in the rebuttal.

- The paper discussed a lot about OLN (Kim et al. 2022). It would be nice if the authors use a short paragraph to summarize the paper first for readers who are not familiar with this work.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: This paper contains a mixture of existing techniques and novel techniques, and is not super clear to assess the contributions. The overall system is a bit complex and the authors did not mention if the code will be available to reproduce.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper works on an interesting problem with a few reasonable technical components. However, the new components are not well ablated or not very clear why they are important. The benchmark/ baselines used in this paper are not the strongest ones for the problem. Based on these drawbacks, I think the paper is not ready to publish in its current status and recommend the authors to prepare a stronger resubmission.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.summary_of_the_paper: Object detection datasets have the inherent issue of having only some classes annotated. Thus, object detection learns to suppress some signals associated to unannotated objects. The method proposes some architectural changes to avoid this. Specifically, they put a stop-gradient to avoid backpropagating the signal from the classification head into the backbone (due to the aforementioned issue of some classes not being annotated) and add an IoU head to play the role that the classification head usually plays. They further use a MoCo adaptation to add contrastive learning to improve the instance representation.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength
The paper uses advanced techniques such as contrastive learning with a queue for patch representation. 
The arguments used to justify their architectural choices seem well grounded and the experiments reflect that.
They show positive results respect to baselines.

Weakness
Strange to me that it tackles open world without language
No baselines include the many open world detectors that have been proposed.
Unclear in key aspects.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
It is unclear to me on Sec. 3.2 the mechanism by which the stop gradient can improve the performance on the new classes. This should be better explained. My understanding is that rather than helping it does not hurt (by removing the mechanism by which it degrades the backbone), but I am not sure why having the classifier vs not having it would change performance if the rest is kept the same.

The setting is pretty unclear throughout the paper. It seems to be that "novel" objects are bundled in a binary class "new object", but this is not clearly stated to the best of my knowledge. I assumed for long parts of the paper that the setting would be few shot detection (which would be amenable to the use of MoCo for object representation). It would make sense to expand on sec. 3.1.

The lack of clarity makes it hard to judge the novelty and reproducibility.
content.summary_of_the_review: Paper with some clarity issues. It also seems like the problem they are tackling can be tackled much better through other technical approaches (based on joint vision and language training), as shown in the several open-world works that have been appearing in the last year or so. But maybe I misunderstood something fundamental.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This work lists down few tricks to build an effective open-world instance recognition model. It builds on top of the existing SoA Deformable-DETR open-set model while overcoming some of the perceived drawbacks.  

First presumption is, that the gradient flow from the classification head has the ability to degrade the feature representations thus making it unsuitable for detecting \textit{novel} objects. In order to overcome this, it borrows simple trick from SimSiam network and applies stop-grad operation to the classification head. This ensures that the model do not improvised features to distinguish between base and novel class.

Since the use of stop-grad also disables the discriminative ability of network against the backdrop, it needs an additional framework to learn the objectness. To this extent it proposes a contrastive learning framework for learning discriminative representations between objects and backdrop. This is achieved by the use of common object representation retrieved from the pooled embeddings of annotated objects which are stored in an object queue.

Finally, the work demonstrates the advantage of pseudo-label transfer for training an existing open-set recognition model. When evaluated on COCO, LVIS, UVO and Objects365, SWORD is shown to achieve SoA results.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1. Comprehensive evaluation on benchmark datasets for open-set setting while beating most of the baseline.
2. Ablation study of design parameters provides an in-depth understanding of what works and what not.

Weaknesses:
1. Technically, the only contribution is the framework for contrastive learning. Other bells and whistles are inspired by previous work. Thus I would expect this framework to be explained in depth. However, I find it difficult to decipher how the contrastive framework is setup (more in the next section). Overall, the writing is poor and many details are missing. It is left to the readers to wiggle out the details from other related works.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
As pointed earlier the quality of writing is poor. Here I list some instances:
1. How is object queue updated ? What I understand is, if there is only single query in the form of average-pooled object center, then using eq. (1) all the parameters in the queue should be equally updated ? 
2. The object queries output from the transformer are divided into positive and negative proposals ? And this selection is based on simple matching score in eq (3) ? How is k1, k2 selected ?
3. Eq (3) seems to be a simple matching cost. Why is termed as optimal transport selection problem ? How is matching performed ? Hungarian loss as DETR ?
4. Not clear to me how are IoU scores retrieved. Because it says it is supervised by binary CE loss. Isn't IoU scores are real values ?
5. Moreover, it wasn't clear to me what actually $AR_{10}$ or $AR_{100}$ means until I dug into the literature. 
6. What is one-to-many label assignment ? This concept was introduced during the ablation study. Until then, readers are not aware that model uses this technique.

In its current version, model seems quite difficult to reproduce.
content.summary_of_the_review: In summary, I should say the model is well engineered and thus achieves SoA on open-set instance recognition setup. However, the technical contribution is weak and writing is not on par with ICLR standard.
